source.note: Screenshots were supplied by Brice in the coaching conversation. Public study should summarize the evidence without republishing the private messages.

points.context: Saturday early-morning message; sequence is before the later long-run-linked reading, but pre-run status is not independently verified.
Saturday later reading; athlete says it was after breakfast, and the conversation links the drop to the long run.
Athlete reports first thing in the morning after a full night's sleep; exact clock time and bathroom/hydration conditions are not independently verified.

body_mass.saturday_interpretation: The 5.0 lb same-day swing is not treated as fat or tissue loss. It shows large acute scale variability around the long run, with fluid, glycogen, gut content and measurement conditions plausible contributors.
body_mass.interpretation: The 163.2 lb reading is a useful morning checkpoint, but the weekend swings are too large to interpret as tissue gain. A sequence of comparable morning readings plus repeat tape measurements is required.

running_and_recovery_context.prior_quality_session: 12 x 400 m reported mostly in the 70s, closing in 69 s, versus approximately 82 s prescribed by his running coach.
running_and_recovery_context.mobility_self_massage_adherence: Coach reports Adrian had not been doing his mobility or self-massage work consistently.
running_and_recovery_context.walking_strategy: Athlete had been using roughly one-hour walks on many days in an attempt to loosen his calves.
running_and_recovery_context.saturday_long_run_response: After the Saturday long run, coach reports the calves were extremely tender to touch and massage, to the point Adrian was nearly in tears.
coach_decision: Stop using one-hour walks as the default calf-loosening strategy.
Use lower-load recovery such as yin yoga / gentle mobility instead, without forcing painful calf range.
Resume recovery and self-care work rather than stacking more locomotor load onto already irritated calves.
If workload rises, add a few hundred calories around the harder sessions rather than leaving intake unchanged.
running_and_recovery_context.medical_boundary: This record describes coaching observations and athlete reports, not a diagnosis. Persistent severe tenderness, swelling, weakness, dark urine, inability to walk normally, or worsening one-sided symptoms would warrant medical assessment.

nutrition_adherence.athlete_report: Getting calories in now feels easy. Before this coaching phase he was often snacking rather than eating full meals; he is surprised he can reach the intended intake with regular full meals and does not mind eating.
nutrition_adherence.interpretation: This is a meaningful adherence signal. It does not establish measured energy surplus or hypertrophy by itself.
nutrition_adherence.hard_day_adjustment: Coach allows a few hundred additional calories around harder or higher-workload sessions; this is a contextual workload adjustment, not a new fixed daily target.

next_evidence: Repeat waist, chest, relaxed arm, relaxed thigh and calf measurements using the September 24 method.
Collect 1-3 comparable morning weights per week under similar conditions.
Record calf tenderness, walking comfort and next-run response after the recovery adjustment.
Keep the 12 x 400 m departure from prescription connected to the recovery record rather than treating it as a performance win in isolation.
Record actual hard-day intake when the extra calories are used.
scope: Study evidence and public-study projection. No completed workout is invented; no medical diagnosis is made; prior measurements and weight reports remain preserved.
